newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Brussels bourse fall rattles nerves pre-holiday.
newsitem.headline: Brussels bourse fall rattles nerves pre-holiday.

text.p: Belgian shares were hit on Wednesday, the last day of the two-week forward market account, by a bout of profit-taking which left some players wondering if the recent record run had come to a temporary end.

The Bel-20 leading share index ended down 19.12 points, or 0.85 percent, at 2,234.75 points, just off its session-low of 2,233.79. The index is due to drop another 13.5 points at the start of trade on Friday -- after Thursday's Ascension holiday -- due to dividend payments.
"It does not look good for the days ahead," one trader said. "Normally we should have been higher these past two days."
"There's been a big seller in the market for the last two or three days," another trader said, suggesting arbitrage between cash and futures positions was to blame.
The number of futures contracts traded on Wednesday fell, he said, indicating maybe one player was taking profits after the bourse's recent record run.
The Bel-20 index rose 4.62 percent in April, ending the month 18.47 percent above 1996's closing level, the Brussels Stock Exchange said on Wednesday.
"But I was surprised to see all the stocks going ex-dividend on Friday being sold today," he added.
Stocks going ex-dividend include Kredietbank which ended down 250 francs at 13,825 francs and Generale Bank, which lost 75 francs to 14,800 francs.
Elsewhere, steel stocks were in focus following news from Luxembourg's Arbed group late Tuesday that it saw an improvement in prospects for the second half of 1997.

"It's not only Arbed that's saying this...we are getting more positive again on the sector," one trader said, saying his house two weeks ago raised Belgian Cockerill to "buy" from "hold". Arbed rose 30 francs to 3,530 francs. Cockerill fell one franc at 133 francs.
Cement maker CBR, one of the market's fastest recent risers, slipped 2.79 percent to 3,490 francs. The company told its annual shareholders meeting it expected 1997 results in line with 1996.
Fast food chain Quick bucked the market trend, continuing to benefit from a broker upgrade on Monday, rising 4.80 percent to 1,965 francs.

The move failed to help Quick parent company GIB, a Bel-20 component, which fell 25 francs to 1,555 francs. After the close of trade GIB said it would raise its 1996 net dividend 6.7 percent to 31.50 francs, payable from June 25.
